title: The rights and wrongs of science

paragraphs.text: There are millions of scientists in the world but, despite this, few cases of major scientific corruption have ever been uncovered. It is unlikely, therefore, that many scientists will have been involved in them. Nevertheless, at the day-to-day level ethical problems still arise, and I shall consider some of the most common and look at what usually happens.

Some of the most spectacular problems arise in academic science. In principle, academic science is a self-regulating professional system where scientists produce knowledge and, if it is considered acceptable, it is then published in journals and rigorously reviewed by fellow-scientists. To have a chance of moving up the career ladder, a scientist needs to have a sufficient record of papers published in reputable scientific journals.

The reality is less clear. Science is a career, and ambitious people are tempted to cut corners and perhaps behave improperly to achieve success. Let us look at some of the ways in which this is done.

The most common temptation that scientists fall victim to is claiming results that were not produced by experiments. This can happen if a cherished theory is not in fact supported by evidence. The case of William Summerlin is a good example. Summerlin seemed to have made a breakthrough in research on the transplanting of organs. His boss, a hard-driving researcher, trumpeted his results across the nation, but Summerlin was unable to produce the results expected. Eventually, he crudely faked results supporting his theory, and was caught out.

More disturbing are cases such as those of John Spector and John Darsee. Both these young researchers built up huge lists of publications and seemed headed for brilliant careers in science. Spector, at Cornell University, was known as a brilliant experimentalist and appeared to be discovering mechanisms by which cancers work. Darsee published nearly 100 papers and abstracts in a single year at Harvard University. However, fellow researchers became suspicious of this high productivity and eventually, after extensive investigations, both researchers lost their jobs.

Scientific fraud is quite unacceptable but an important point emerges from reading about these cases: it is very hard to expose a scientific fraud. It requires sustained efforts by a whistleblower before anyone takes any notice.

Plagiarism is taking work, and credit for it, from its rightful owner. Sometimes this is simple theft but sometimes it is more like extortion. An example of the former is the case of Heinrich Wachtslicht-Rodbard. This young researcher wrote a paper and submitted it to an important journal. After a reasonable interval, comments came back from referees indicating that, with some revisions, the paper might be acceptable. Dr Wachtslicht-Rodbard was revising the paper when another journal paper caught his eye. It contained whole sections of his work, his data and even his ways of phrasing things. Naturally, he complained, but it took months of badgering senior scientists before anything was done. One reason for this was the standing of the authors. One, Vijay Soman, was a young researcher, but the other, Philip Felig, was a professor at Yale University Medical School, and a prominent scientist.

The truth was finally revealed that the younger scientist, Soman, had written the paper based on Wachtslicht-Rodbard’s data. Felig knew very little about it but his name had been added because of their working relationship. This is termed ‘honorary authorship’ and is also counted as dishonesty in science, although many do not regard it as serious. Soman left his job and Felig lost a good deal of prestige. The worst sufferer was the victim, who lost all interest in doing science and left the profession.

can also take the form of extortion. Imagine a junior research worker who has done all the work for a paper. If that research assistant suddenly finds that her boss has put himself down as senior author, claiming the credit that is not his, what can she do about it? Her contract may expire at the end of the year, and her boss will not renew it if she makes a fuss. According to some observers, this sort of unfairness on the part of superiors is quite common.

In this section we will look at a few questionable types of behaviour. Some scientists regard these as wrong, others as perfectly acceptable. Imagine a scientist has done a series of experiments. From 15 results, 14 make good sense while the 15th is an odd result that makes no sense. This sort of thing is fairly common in science. Equipment, for example, can be unreliable. One solution is for the scientist to simply drop the strange result and act as though there were only 14 experiments. Is this fraud? Should the extra result be included?

A second grey area concerns scientists’ desperate need for money to buy equipment, hire assistants, and the like, and can lead scientists to develop skills and tricks to get money from research organisations. One such trick is to put in extra effort and get ahead of where the funding organisation thinks you are by a whole series of experiments. You can then apply for money to do research that has already been done. This procedure has huge advantages. You can give regular reports on the research and guarantee that there will be results to report. Meanwhile, of course, the money is being used to do still more research, so that the process can be repeated – the researcher is assured of a supply of funds, and the funding organisation is getting results for its money. This is a disservice to the scientific community, however, because it is damaging to other researchers.

The aim of tricks and stratagems used in science is always to further the scientist’s career and to give some security in a difficult and uncertain profession. Who decides whether these tricks are acceptable? In theory, other scientists do. In reality, until recently, nobody seemed to worry too much! As we have seen, it was difficult to bring to light cases of quite blatant fraud. It is much harder if the bounds of honesty are debatable.

Scientists are judged by their peers.
